Reproducing Bouabid, Vu et al. (2026) from dandiset 001692¶

Paper. Bouabid S, Vu M-AT, Noggle C, Vietti-Michelina S, Brimblecombe K, Platt N, Zhang L, Joshi A, Cragg S, Howe MW (2026). An anatomical hotspot for striatal dopamine-acetylcholine interactions during reward and movement. bioRxiv. doi:10.64898/2026.01.20.700614. This attempt used the full text of the preprint (version 1, CC-BY).

Dandiset. DANDI:001692, version 0.260303.1724. The paper's Key Resources Table (Zenodo doi:10.5281/zenodo.18202873) and its code's README cite this version, which is also the only published one, so it is pinned here.

What the dandiset holds. Multi-fiber photometry of DA (GRAB-rDA3m, red) and ACh (GRAB-ACh3.0, green) in head-fixed mice: spontaneous and unpredicted-reward sessions of 5 mice (UG27 to UG31, Figures 1 to 3, 5 and 6), Pavlovian sessions of 3 mice (AD1 to AD3, Figure 4), sessions of 3 control mice with non-functional sensors (AD4 to AD6, Extended Data Figure 1), and stimulation sessions of 6 DAT-cre mice (ADS*, Figure 7). The ex vivo slice data of Figure 8 are not in it; their source data are on Zenodo and are used for the Figure 8 claims.

Code read. The paper's analysis code, github.com/HoweLab/BouabidVu2026 at commit 833fa3d (MATLAB). Where the Methods leave a choice open the code's choice is followed; where they disagree the Methods are followed and the code's choice is a variant.

import time
import warnings

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.api as sm
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
from scipy import stats

import daach

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", category=RuntimeWarning)
pd.set_option("display.width", 200)
pd.set_option("display.max_columns", 40)
pd.set_option("display.max_rows", 200)
started = time.time()

assets = daach.list_assets()
subject_of = lambda a: a["path"].split("/")[0][4:]
UG = [a for a in assets if subject_of(a).startswith("UG")]
ADS = [a for a in assets if subject_of(a).startswith("ADS")]
AD = [a for a in assets if subject_of(a).startswith("AD") and not subject_of(a).startswith("ADS")]

ug = daach.load_many(UG, series="hp_art")
ad_events = daach.load_many(AD, func=daach.read_events)
ads = daach.load_many(ADS, series="raw")


def light_reward_fraction(e):
    ev = e["events"]
    if "Light" not in ev:
        return np.nan
    rewards = ev["Reward"][0] if "Reward" in ev else np.array([])
    return np.mean([((rewards > a) & (rewards < b)).any() for a, b in zip(*ev["Light"])])


pav_table = pd.DataFrame([{"path": e["path"], "mouse": e["subject"], "session": e["session_id"],
                           "indicators": "+".join(e["indicators"]), "events": ",".join(sorted(e["events"])),
                           "n_light": len(e["events"].get("Light", ([],))[0]),
                           "n_reward": len(e["events"].get("Reward", ([],))[0]),
                           "light_rewarded": light_reward_fraction(e)} for e in ad_events])
by_path = {a["path"]: a for a in assets}
selected = []
for m in ("AD1", "AD2", "AD3"):
    t = pav_table[pav_table.mouse == m].sort_values("session")
    selected += [(p, "learning") for p in t[t.light_rewarded == 1.0].path.iloc[-3:]]
    selected += [(p, "extinction") for p in t[np.isclose(t.light_rewarded, 0.2)].path.iloc[-3:]]
pav = daach.load_many([by_path[p] for p, _ in selected], series="hp")
for s, (_, phase) in zip(pav, selected):
    s["phase"] = phase
control_paths = pav_table[pav_table.mouse.isin(["AD4", "AD5", "AD6"]) & (pav_table.n_light == 0)
                          & (pav_table.n_reward > 0)].path
ctrl = daach.load_many([by_path[p] for p in control_paths], series="hp")
print(f"{len(assets)} assets in dandiset {daach.DANDISET_ID} version {daach.DANDISET_VERSION}; streamed "
      f"{len(ug)} UG, {len(ad_events)} AD event tables, {len(pav)} Pavlovian, {len(ctrl)} control and "
      f"{len(ads)} ADS sessions in {time.time() - started:.0f} s")

339 assets in dandiset 001692 version 0.260303.1724; streamed 105 UG, 211 AD event tables, 18 Pavlovian, 15 control and 23 ADS sessions in 224 s

Data check¶

Each check of the metadata against the values is stated under its output.

Som'

The files of AD4 to AD6 name the mutant ACh sensor and tdTomato; all others name ACh3.0 and rDA3m. The files call the mutant sensor ACh4.3mut (device and surgery text), where the Methods and the Key Resources Table name ACh3.0-mut. The description of the 470 nm source describes a different setup (470 and 405 nm alternated at 100 Hz, with an isosbestic control), and that of the 570 nm source reads "405 nm"; the Methods alternate 470 and 570 nm at 36 Hz. The session description gives 9 uL rewards at 5 to 30 s intervals, where the Methods give 5 uL at 10 to 30 s, and its micro sign is stored mis-encoded ("9 Î¼L"). The cohorts are told apart only by subject name and indicator; no field in the files states the experiment or the figure a session belongs to. UG29's session 240308 has licks but no rewards and is treated as spontaneous, as its name has no r.

Included sites per cohort: {'ADS': 180, 'Pavlovian': 75, 'UG': 174, 'control': 125}
Paper: 174 sites in 5 mice (Figures 1-3, 5, 6); 75 sites in 3 mice (Figure 4); 180 sites in 6 mice (Figure 7).

The included sites match the paper's counts: 174 for UG27 to UG31, 75 for AD1 to AD3 and 180 for the six ADS mice. The fiber coordinates (mm from bregma, AP, ML and DV) are the same in every session of a mouse, which is consistent with each site being the same fiber across sessions; the analysis treats it so, as the paper does, and the per-mouse breakdowns below are the check on pooling. All sites lie in the right hemisphere (ML 0.37 to 3.74 mm).

Sessions whose photometry and behavior sample counts differ: 0

Every photometry series states a rate of 9.0 Hz, but each has as many samples as the behavior series, starts at the behavior's first timestamp, and the behavior timestamps step by 55.6 ms (18.0 Hz). The Methods give 18 Hz per channel and the code uses sr = 18. At the stated rate the recordings would last twice as long as their timestamps. The data support 18 Hz; it is used throughout, and the stated rate is a metadata error. The red series starts 27.5 ms (half a sample) before the green, as the alternating excitation implies; DA and ACh are paired by sample index, as in the code.

The dF/F values are small fractions, as dF/F should be (1st to 99th percentiles between -0.033 and 0.040). The artifact-removed series holds NaNs where artifacts were cut. Some control sites have a constant red trace in some sessions; their correlation is undefined there and is averaged over the other sessions. Wheel velocity is in m/s with plausible values (99th percentiles 0.13 to 0.47 m/s). The mice differ in how much they run: the smoothed velocity exceeds the stillness threshold 11% to 79% of the time.

Pavlovian sessions fall into three groups by the fraction of light cues followed by a reward: 1.0 (learning), 0.2 (light cue extinguished) and 0.8 (tone cue extinguished). Learning sessions have 68 rewards: 30 after light cues, 30 after tone cues and 8 uncued, as the Methods describe. The files hold no tone cue events, so tone trials cannot be analysed; the paper's Figure 4 uses light trials only, as its code shows. Which phase a session belongs to is not stated in the files and is inferred here from the events.

def fingerprint(s):
    return (len(s["DA"]), tuple(np.round(np.nan_to_num(s["DA"][:200, :3]).ravel(), 6)))

seen, dups = {}, []

    if k in seen:
        dups.append((seen[k], s["path"]))
    seen[k] = s["path"]

      "none share traces (above)")

In [9]:
def response_contrast(sessions, events_of, shift_s=10.0):
    # mean over sites of |mean dF/F 0-1 s minus -0.5-0 s| at the events and at events shifted later
    out = []
    for m, ss in daach.by_mouse(sessions).items():
        vals = {"true": [], "shifted": []}
        for s in ss:
            e = events_of(s)
            for key, ev in (("true", e), ("shifted", e + int(shift_s * daach.SR))):
                ev = ev[(ev > 9) & (ev < len(s["DA"]) - 19)]
                if not len(ev):
                    continue
                for ch in ("DA", "ACh"):
                    r = daach.raster(s[ch], ev, -9, 18)
                    mu = np.nanmean(r, 2)
                    vals[key].append(np.nanmean(np.abs(mu[9:].mean(0) - mu[:9].mean(0))))
        out.append({"mouse": m, "true": np.mean(vals["true"]), "shifted_10s": np.mean(vals["shifted"])})
    return pd.DataFrame(out)

checks = {
    "reward sessions, first lick": (reward, lambda s: daach.first_licks(s)[1]),
    "Pavlovian, light cue": (pav, lambda s: daach.event_index(s, s["events"]["Light"][0])),
    "ADS, stimulation": (ads, lambda s: daach.event_index(s, s["events"]["Optogenetic Stimulation"][0])),
    "spontaneous, initiation": (spont, lambda s: daach.initiations(daach.smooth_velocity(s["velocity"]))[0]),
}
for name, (ss, f) in checks.items():
    t = response_contrast(ss, f)
    t["ratio"] = t.true / t.shifted_10s
    print(name)
    print(t.round(4).to_string(index=False))

For every mouse and each kind of event, the photometry response in the second after the event is larger at the event times than at times shifted by 10 s (the ratios above), so the events, the velocity and the photometry share one clock in every cohort. This shows alignment to within the response's time scale (about a second); finer offsets would not show here.

fig1e-dominant-polarity¶

Across 174 sites in 5 mice, the dominant DA-ACh cross-correlation during spontaneous behavior is negative at 132 sites, 127 of them with DA leading, and positive at 42 sites, 31 of them with ACh leading.

    return {"negative": int((dom < 0).sum()), "negative, DA leads": int(((dom < 0) & (lag > 0)).sum()),
            "positive": int((dom > 0).sum()), "positive, ACh leads": int(((dom > 0) & (lag < 0)).sum()),
            "lag 0": int((lag == 0).sum()), "sites": len(dom)}

Result: reproduced. Of 174 sites, the dominant correlation is negative at 133 (128 with DA leading) and positive at 41 (32 with ACh leading), against 132, 127, 42 and 31 in the paper; all four are within 10%. Every mouse has more negative than positive sites. Correlating concatenated sessions gives the same counts except 30 positive sites with ACh leading.

fig1f-adls-hotspot¶

The dominant correlations form a significant hotspot, identified by local Moran's I, in the anterior dorsolateral striatum (aDLS), where the strongest correlations are negative.

The hotspot procedure is fixed in the claims file: linear interpolation onto a 100 um grid, padding, Gaussian smoothing, local Moran's I against 200 shuffles of the values across sites, the 95th percentile, and the connected volume of at least 0.125 mm3 with the largest mean magnitude. One grid is shared by all cohorts so that sites of other cohorts can be placed in this hotspot.

def show_map(hs, title, vmax=0.5):
    vol = hs["smooth"]
    mask = np.zeros(GRID.shape, bool)
    if hs["voxels"] is not None:
        mask.ravel()[hs["voxels"]] = True
    fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8, 3.5))
    ap, ml, dv = GRID.axes
    axs[0].imshow(np.nanmean(vol, 2), origin="lower", cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-vmax, vmax=vmax, aspect="auto",
                  extent=[ml[0], ml[-1], ap[0], ap[-1]])
    axs[0].contour(ml, ap, mask.any(2), levels=[0.5], colors="k")
    axs[0].set_xlabel("ML (mm)"); axs[0].set_ylabel("AP (mm)"); axs[0].set_title("axial, mean projection")
    im = axs[1].imshow(np.nanmean(vol, 1).T, origin="lower", cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-vmax, vmax=vmax, aspect="auto",
                       extent=[ap[0], ap[-1], dv[0], dv[-1]])
    axs[1].contour(ap, dv, mask.any(1).T, levels=[0.5], colors="k")
    axs[1].set_xlabel("AP (mm)"); axs[1].set_ylabel("DV (mm)"); axs[1].set_title("sagittal, mean projection")
    axs[1].invert_xaxis()
    fig.colorbar(im, ax=axs, shrink=0.8)
    fig.suptitle(title)
    plt.show()
    print(f"Smoothed values range {np.nanmin(vol):.3f} to {np.nanmax(vol):.3f}; color scale clipped at +/-{vmax}; "
          f"voxels beyond it: {int((np.abs(vol) > vmax).sum())} of {int((~np.isnan(vol)).sum())}")

show_map(hs1, "Dominant spontaneous DA-ACh r; black, hotspot")

Smoothed values range -0.473 to 0.105; color scale clipped at +/-0.5; voxels beyond it: 0 of 6155

Result: partially reproduced. A significant hotspot is found (1.01 mm3) with a negative mean smoothed r (-0.368, against -0.185 over the hull). Its centroid (AP 0.63, ML 2.02, DV -3.14 mm) is anterior and dorsal of the median site (0.10, 2.04, -3.21) but 0.02 mm medial of it, so by the criterion fixed beforehand it is not in the lateral half. With the 99th percentile of the null the hotspot shrinks to 518 voxels and its centroid moves to ML 2.09 mm, lateral of the median. Sites of all five mice fall inside it (28 sites). Finding a hotspot is not evidence on its own: with the values shuffled across sites the procedure finds one in 67 of 100 shuffles. None of those is as large as the real one (at most 482 voxels against 1010) or has a mean as low (-0.368).

Result: not reproduced. In the control mice the hotspot procedure finds a hotspot (mean smoothed r +0.33, 551 voxels, centroid AP 0.68, ML 1.29, DV -4.14 mm). The procedure finds a hotspot in 73 of 100 shuffles of the control values, but none of those reaches 551 voxels (31 have a mean of at least +0.33), so by the paper's own test the control correlations are organized in space. The correlations are mostly positive (68% of 124 sites, median r 0.20) but not weak: the median |r| is 0.238, as in the sensor mice (0.240), and 65% of control sites exceed |r| = 0.2 against 54% of sensor sites. Two differences from the paper's method could add correlated red-green signal here: the control files hold no artifact-removed series, so the high-pass series is used without artifact removal, and the test used the 15 uncued reward sessions of these mice, not all of their ITI data.

                 "wilcoxon_p": stats.wilcoxon(di).pvalue})
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False))
print("\nMedian directionality index by mouse (negative: DA leads):")

Result: reproduced. For each pair type the occurrence hotspot shares 780 to 826 voxels with the correlation hotspot, against null medians of 88 to 111, with overlap p of 0.005, 0.015, 0.005 and below 0.005 (the paper 0.005, 0.005, 0.002 and below 0.001). The occurrence hotspots have centroids at AP 0.59 to 0.64, ML 1.87 to 2.05 and DV -3.13 to -3.17 mm, and occurrence is higher inside the correlation hotspot than outside for each type (rank-sum p < 0.001). After subtracting the chance occurrence (DA and ACh transients from different sessions of the same site, 10 shuffles), every site keeps an excess for every type (medians 0.08 to 0.11), the excess is higher inside the correlation hotspot (p < 0.001), and its hotspots overlap the correlation hotspot with p of 0.030, 0.005, 0.015 and below 0.005.

After unpredicted rewards, trial-by-trial DA peak magnitude correlates with ACh; dominant correlations are negative at 114 of 174 sites with DA leading (177.9 +/- 96.7 ms) and positive at 58 of 174 with ACh leading (-41.2 +/- 218.9 ms).

assert np.allclose(coords3, coords1)

def corr_summary(dom, lat):
    neg, pos = dom < 0, dom > 0
    return {"sites": int((~np.isnan(dom)).sum()), "negative": int(neg.sum()), "negative_lag>0": int((neg & (lat > 0)).sum()),
            "mean_latency_negative_ms": lat[neg].mean(), "sd_negative": lat[neg].std(ddof=1),
            "positive": int(pos.sum()), "positive_lag<0": int((pos & (lat < 0)).sum()),
            "mean_latency_positive_ms": lat[pos].mean(), "sd_positive": lat[pos].std(ddof=1)}

s3 = corr_summary(dom3, lat3)

fig4-cue-sequence¶

After Pavlovian conditioning, the conditioned light cue evokes an ACh peak, then a DA peak, then an ACh dip at a majority of sites (49 of 75).

In [26]:
W4 = (-9, 54)
IDX4 = np.arange(W4[0], W4[1] + 1)


def light_events(s):
    return daach.event_index(s, s["events"]["Light"][0])


def iti_exclusion(s):
    cues = light_events(s)
    rew = daach.event_index(s, s["events"]["Reward"][0])
    return [(i, i + int(9 * daach.SR)) for i in cues] + [(i, i + int(5 * daach.SR)) for i in rew]


learn = [s for s in pav if s["phase"] == "learning"]
ext = [s for s in pav if s["phase"] == "extinction"]
rng = np.random.default_rng(401)
er4 = daach.event_rasters(learn, light_events, *W4, exclude_of=iti_exclusion)
sig4 = {w: daach.triggered_significance(er4, *W4, w, rng) for w in ((9, 27), (9, 36))}
mice4, coords4 = daach.site_table(learn)


def sequence(sig, rows, alpha="methods"):
    out = []
    for m in sorted(sig):
        a, d = sig[m]["ACh"], sig[m]["DA"]
        ap, an = a[alpha]
        dp, _ = d[alpha]
        w = slice(rows[0], rows[1] + 1)
        ta, td, tn = np.argmax(a["mean"][w], 0), np.argmax(d["mean"][w], 0), np.argmin(a["mean"][w], 0)
        out.append(ap & dp & an & (ta < td) & (td < tn))
    return np.concatenate(out)

for label, rows in (("(a) 0 to 1 s", (9, 27)), ("(b) 0 to 1.5 s", (9, 36))):
    seq = sequence(sig4[rows], rows)
    seq_code = sequence(sig4[rows], rows, "code")
    print(f"Reading {label}: sequence at {int(seq.sum())} of {len(seq)} sites; by mouse "
          f"{pd.Series(seq).groupby(mice4).sum().to_dict()}; code percentiles {int(seq_code.sum())}")
s = sig4[(9, 27)]
print("Significant features in 0 to 1 s (Methods percentiles):",
      {k: int(daach.stack(s, f).sum()) for k, f in (("ACh peak", lambda v: v["ACh"]["methods"][0]),
                                                  ("ACh dip", lambda v: v["ACh"]["methods"][1]),
                                                  ("DA peak", lambda v: v["DA"]["methods"][0]))})
print("Light-cue trials per mouse:", {m: len(d["events"]) for m, d in er4.items()})

Reading (a) 0 to 1 s: sequence at 58 of 75 sites; by mouse {'AD1': 12, 'AD2': 19, 'AD3': 27}; code percentiles 55
Reading (b) 0 to 1.5 s: sequence at 58 of 75 sites; by mouse {'AD1': 12, 'AD2': 19, 'AD3': 27}; code percentiles 52
Significant features in 0 to 1 s (Methods percentiles): {'ACh peak': 68, 'ACh dip': 72, 'DA peak': 75}
Light-cue trials per mouse: {'AD1': 90, 'AD2': 90, 'AD3': 90}

Result: not reproduced. The light cue evokes an ACh peak, then a DA peak, then an ACh dip at 58 of 75 sites under both readings, more than the paper's 49 and above the tolerance (44.1 to 53.9). The statement's qualitative part holds: the sequence is at a majority of sites overall and in each mouse (12 of 17, 19 of 24, 27 of 34). With the code's percentiles the count is 55 or 52.

Result: partially reproduced. All 75 sites have a significant cue DA peak, so both readings give the same values: 41 negative sites with a mean latency of 206.0 ms (the paper 39 and 202.28 ms) and 34 positive sites with a mean latency of -83.3 ms (the paper 26 and -79.1 ms). Three values are within tolerance; the positive count is above its range (23.4 to 28.6). ACh lags at 37 of the 41 negative sites and leads at 22 of the 34 positive ones. The code's percentiles also find a cue DA peak at all 75 sites; the null is drawn from about 69000 to 74000 candidate times per mouse, so its size does not explain the paper's 65.

After cue-specific extinction, cue-evoked DA dips correlate negatively with lagging ACh at 41 of 74 sites, mean lag 117.9 +/- 176.2 ms.

fig5d-initiation-responses¶

At locomotion initiations, ACh rises and then falls at 131 of 174 sites; DA dips at 119 of 174 sites, rises at 73, and both rises and dips at 32.

In [31]:
W5 = (-18, 36)
IDX5 = np.arange(W5[0], W5[1] + 1)
SIG5 = (9, 36)  # rows for -0.5 to 1 s


def init_rasters(loco):
    out = {}
    for m, d in loco.items():
        samp = daach.sampleable_times(len(d["vel"]), *W5, valid=~np.isnan(d["vel"]))
        samp = np.setdiff1d(samp, d["init"])
        out[m] = {"cat": d["cat"], "events": d["init"], "sampleable": samp,
                  "rasters": {k: daach.raster(d["cat"][k], d["init"], *W5) for k in ("DA", "ACh")}}
    return out


def init_counts(sig, alpha="methods"):
    dp = daach.stack(sig, lambda v: v["DA"][alpha][0]); dn = daach.stack(sig, lambda v: v["DA"][alpha][1])
    ap = daach.stack(sig, lambda v: v["ACh"][alpha][0]); an = daach.stack(sig, lambda v: v["ACh"][alpha][1])
    ta = daach.stack(sig, lambda v: np.argmax(v["ACh"]["mean"][SIG5[0]:SIG5[1] + 1], 0))
    tn = daach.stack(sig, lambda v: np.argmin(v["ACh"]["mean"][SIG5[0]:SIG5[1] + 1], 0))
    return {"ACh rise then fall (a)": int((ap & an & (ta < tn)).sum()), "ACh rise (b)": int(ap.sum()),
            "DA dip": int(dn.sum()), "DA rise": int(dp.sum()), "DA both": int((dp & dn).sum()),
            "ACh dip": int(an.sum()), "ACh both, any order": int((ap & an).sum())}

loco = daach.locomotion_events(spont)
print("Initiations (bout >= 2.27 s) per mouse:", {m: len(d["init"]) for m, d in loco.items()},
      "; all clean onsets:", {m: len(d["init_all"]) for m, d in loco.items()})
er5 = init_rasters(loco)
sig5 = daach.triggered_significance(er5, *W5, SIG5, np.random.default_rng(501))
c5 = init_counts(sig5)
print("Counts (Methods percentiles):", c5)
exp5 = {"DA dip": 119, "DA rise": 73, "DA both": 32}
print("Within 10%:", {k: abs(c5[k] - v) <= 0.1 * v for k, v in exp5.items()},
      "; ACh (a)", abs(c5["ACh rise then fall (a)"] - 131) <= 13.1, "; ACh (b)", abs(c5["ACh rise (b)"] - 131) <= 13.1)
print("Variant, code percentiles (0.5/99.5):", init_counts(sig5, "code"))
mice5 = np.concatenate([[m] * d["cat"]["DA"].shape[1] for m, d in loco.items()])
per5 = pd.DataFrame([{"mouse": m, **init_counts({m: sig5[m]})} for m in sig5])
print(per5.to_string(index=False))
loco22 = daach.locomotion_events(spont, bout_s=2.2)
sig22 = daach.triggered_significance(init_rasters(loco22), *W5, SIG5, np.random.default_rng(502))
print("Variant, the code's bout of 2.2 s:", {m: len(d["init"]) for m, d in loco22.items()}, init_counts(sig22))

fig5-latency-order¶

Initiation-related signals occur in sequence; DA dips first (median 111.11 ms), then ACh peaks (222.22 ms) and DA peaks (227.78 ms), then ACh dips (611.11 ms).

In [33]:
def latencies(sig, alpha="methods"):
    out = {}
    for ch in ("DA", "ACh"):
        mean = np.concatenate([sig[m][ch]["mean"] for m in sorted(sig)], 1)[SIG5[0]:SIG5[1] + 1]
        t = IDX5[SIG5[0]:SIG5[1] + 1] * 1000 / 18
        pk = daach.stack(sig, lambda v: v[ch][alpha][0]); dp = daach.stack(sig, lambda v: v[ch][alpha][1])
        out[f"{ch} peak"] = t[np.argmax(mean, 0)][pk]
        out[f"{ch} dip"] = t[np.argmin(mean, 0)][dp]
    return out

lat5 = latencies(sig5)
exp_l = {"DA dip": 111.11, "ACh peak": 222.22, "DA peak": 227.78, "ACh dip": 611.11}

         "paper": exp_l[k], "within_55.6ms": abs(np.median(v) - exp_l[k]) <= 55.6} for k, v in lat5.items()]
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False))
m_ = {k: np.median(v) for k, v in lat5.items()}
print("Order DA dip < ACh peak, DA peak < ACh dip:", m_["DA dip"] < min(m_["ACh peak"], m_["DA peak"]) and
      max(m_["ACh peak"], m_["DA peak"]) < m_["ACh dip"])
print("By mouse (median ms):")
print(pd.DataFrame({m: {k: np.median(v) if len(v) else np.nan for k, v in latencies({m: sig5[m]}).items()} for m in sig5}).round(1).to_string())
print("Variant, code percentiles:", {k: round(float(np.median(v)), 1) for k, v in latencies(sig5, "code").items()})

W7 = (-9, 45)
SIG7 = (7, 45)  # rows for -2 to 36 samples


def iti_stims(s):
    st = daach.event_index(s, s["events"]["Optogenetic Stimulation"][0])
    rew = daach.event_index(s, s["events"]["Reward"][0])
    return np.array([i for i in st if not (np.abs(rew - i) <= 18).any()], int)


def stim_exclusion(s):
    rew, lick = daach.first_licks(s)
    st = daach.event_index(s, s["events"]["Optogenetic Stimulation"][0])
    return ([(i, i + int(5 * daach.SR) + 1) for i in np.concatenate([rew, lick])] + [(i, i + 19) for i in st])

er7 = daach.event_rasters(ads, iti_stims, *W7, exclude_of=stim_exclusion)
sig7 = daach.triggered_significance(er7, *W7, SIG7, np.random.default_rng(701))

      "; all trains:", {m: int(sum(len(s["events"]["Optogenetic Stimulation"][0]) for s in v)) for m, v in daach.by_mouse(ads).items()})

ed9-cohort-hotspot¶

The stimulation cohort replicates the aDLS anti-correlation hotspot in spontaneous release outside stimulation periods.

In [40]:
def ads_mask(mode):
    def f(s):
        n = len(s["DA"])
        rew, lick = daach.first_licks(s)
        st = daach.event_index(s, s["events"]["Optogenetic Stimulation"][0])
        a, b, c = daach.time_since(n, rew) < 6, daach.time_since(n, lick) < 6, daach.time_since(n, st) < 3
        return (a & b & c) if mode == "and" else (a | b | c)
    return f

frac = {mode: sum(int(ads_mask(mode)(s).sum()) for s in ads) / sum(len(s["DA"]) for s in ads) for mode in ("and", "or")}
print(f"Fraction of samples left out: AND {frac['and']:.4f}, OR {frac['or']:.4f}")
def post_stim(s):
    return daach.time_since(len(s["DA"]), daach.event_index(s, s["events"]["Optogenetic Stimulation"][0])) < 3
kept = {mode: sum(int((post_stim(s) & ~ads_mask(mode)(s)).sum()) for s in ads) / sum(int(post_stim(s).sum()) for s in ads)
        for mode in ("and", "or")}
print(f"Fraction of samples within 3 s after stimulation that are kept: AND {kept['and']:.4f}, OR {kept['or']:.4f}")
xc9 = daach.spontaneous_xcorr(ads, mask=ads_mask("and"), concatenate=True)
dom9, lag9 = xc9["dominant"], xc9["lag"]
print("Cohort counts (code's AND exclusion):", polarity_counts(dom9, lag9))
in9 = daach.inside(GRID, hs1, coords_s)
print("Sites inside the original hotspot:", int(in9.sum()), "by mouse", pd.Series(in9).groupby(mice_s).sum().to_dict())
print("(i) in vs out of the original hotspot:", daach.in_out(dom9, in9))
interp9 = daach.Interpolator(GRID, coords_s)
rng = np.random.default_rng(901)
hs9 = daach.hotspot(interp9, dom9, rng)
ov9 = daach.overlap_test(hs1, interp1.inside, hs9, interp9.inside, GRID.shape, rng)
print(f"(ii) cohort hotspot: mean {hs9['mean']:.3f}, voxels {ov9['n_b']}, centroid {hs9['centroid'].round(2)}; overlap", ov9)
xc9o = daach.spontaneous_xcorr(ads, mask=ads_mask("or"), concatenate=True)
print("Variant, OR exclusion:", polarity_counts(xc9o["dominant"], xc9o["lag"]), daach.in_out(xc9o["dominant"], in9))
hs9o = daach.hotspot(interp9, xc9o["dominant"], rng)
print(f"Variant, OR exclusion hotspot: mean {hs9o['mean']:.3f}, centroid {hs9o['centroid'].round(2)}; overlap",
      daach.overlap_test(hs1, interp1.inside, hs9o, interp9.inside, GRID.shape, rng))

Result: partially reproduced. In the stimulation cohort, the 9 sites inside the original hotspot have more negative dominant correlations (median -0.42) than the 171 outside (-0.30), p = 0.049 (exact p = 0.048); the OR exclusion gives p = 0.041. The cohort's own hotspot is negative (mean -0.44, 1536 voxels, centroid AP 0.71, ML 2.00, DV -3.45 mm) and shares 564 voxels with the original against a null median of 65, but the overlap test gives p = 0.085. 167 of the 180 sites have a dominant negative correlation. The code's AND exclusion leaves out 6.5% of samples and the OR exclusion 32.7%. Of the samples within 3 s after a stimulation, AND keeps 42% and OR none; with OR the cohort hotspot is similar (mean -0.41, centroid AP 0.72, ML 2.08, DV -3.43 mm) and its overlap p is also 0.085.

Result: reproduced. ACh minima after stimulation are deeper at the 17 sites inside the cohort hotspot (median -0.0179 dF/F) than at the 163 outside (-0.0149), p = 0.0005. The AND exclusion keeps 42% of the samples within 3 s after a stimulation; with the hotspot of the OR exclusion, which leaves them all out, the 19 sites inside also have deeper minima (median -0.0188 against -0.0149, p = 0.0003). Against the original hotspot (9 sites inside) the difference has the same sign but p = 0.094, and the ACh-minimum hotspot's overlap with the cohort hotspot gives p = 0.065, so the claim's second part (the dips' own hotspot overlaps the cohort hotspot) is not supported at p < 0.05; the criterion treats it as a variant. Within each of the six mice the inside sites have lower minima, significantly so in one (ADS19).

fig8b-quinpirole-region¶

Quinpirole suppresses evoked ACh release in DLS and NAcC, more strongly in DLS; region F(1,40) = 105.9, interaction F(4,40) = 3.014, stimulus F(4,40) = 17.80.

The slice data are not in the dandiset. The paper's source data for Figure 8 are on Zenodo (doi:10.5281/zenodo.18202873) and are read from there.

In [42]:
FIG8 = "https://zenodo.org/records/18202873/files/Bouabid_Vu%20%282026%29_Source_Data_Fig8.xlsx?download=1"
fig8 = pd.read_excel(FIG8, sheet_name=None)
print("Sheets:", list(fig8))


def anova(sheet, factor):
    d = fig8[sheet].rename(columns={factor: "g"})
    # Type III sums of squares with sum-to-zero contrasts, as GraphPad Prism (named in the Methods)
    # computes an ordinary two-way ANOVA; the groups are unbalanced in some sheets
    fit = smf.ols("Peak_ACh ~ C(g, Sum) * C(Stim, Sum)", data=d).fit()
    tab = sm.stats.anova_lm(fit, typ=3)
    t2 = sm.stats.anova_lm(smf.ols("Peak_ACh ~ C(g) * C(Stim)", data=d).fit(), typ=2)
    print(sheet, "| rows", len(d), "| slices per group", d.groupby("g").Slice_ID.nunique().to_dict(),
          "| mouse ids per group", d.groupby("g").Mouse_ID.nunique().to_dict(), "| group means", d.groupby("g").Peak_ACh.mean().round(1).to_dict())
    print(tab.round(4).to_string())
    print("Variant, Type II F:", t2.F.dropna().round(3).tolist())
    return tab

t8b = anova("Figure_8b", "Brain_Region")
print(fig8["Figure_8b"].groupby(["Brain_Region", "Slice_ID"]).Stim.apply(list).to_string())

Result: reproduced. The D2R block effect is F = 231.87 in DLS and 32.57 in NAcC (the paper 231.9 and 32.57), and the antagonist raises ACh in both (DLS 32.8 to 78.6, NAcC 74.1 to 107.9). With Type III sums of squares the DLS stimulus F is 34.46, as in the legend (Type II gives 45.04).

fig8c-cocaine-da-similar (blocked)¶

Cocaine elevates evoked DA release to a similar degree in DLS and NAcC (cocaine by region interaction F(8,36) = 0.20).

The sheet Figure_8c_TP holds a voltammogram (voltage and current); Figure_8c_LP and _RP hold mean DA time courses (24 time points) per mouse and condition, three mice per region. The legend's ANOVA has 8 degrees of freedom for cocaine and 36 residual, which fits neither a two-level cocaine factor nor 24 time points, so the test cannot be repeated. Descriptively, the peak DA with cocaine is 1.48 times the control peak on average in both regions (DLS 1.31 to 1.77, NAcC 1.10 to 2.09 per mouse).

Summary¶

A failure to reproduce here may be a failure of this attempt, not of the paper: see the reasoning and the differences from the paper's method.

How the analysis differs from the paper's. The hotspot procedure is a simplified port of the paper's MATLAB pipeline: linear in place of natural-neighbor interpolation, 100 um in place of 50 um voxels, the convex hull of the sites in place of the Allen striatum mask, and 200 in place of 10000 shuffles and random volumes. The chance occurrence of paired transients uses 10 in place of 10000 shuffles of sessions. Bootstrap nulls use 1000 samples in place of 10000. MATLAB's lowpass is replaced by a zero-phase Butterworth filter. Pavlovian phases are inferred from the files' events. The control analysis uses the 15 uncued reward sessions of AD4 to AD6. Pairs of transients are matched by the Methods' rule (the first partner), a simplification of the code's matching. The Figure 8 ANOVAs use Type III sums of squares, as Prism does.

What was found about the dandiset. The photometry series state a rate of 9 Hz; the timestamps, the Methods and the code give 18 Hz. The files do not say which experiment, cohort or Pavlovian phase a session belongs to; this was inferred from subject names, indicators and events. Tone cue events are absent from the Pavlovian files. One reward session of UG27 (240313r) lacks the artifact-removed green series. The site counts match the paper (174, 75 and 180), and the data support every spontaneous, reward and locomotion analysis tested. The excitation source descriptions differ from the Methods (405 nm isosbestic light at 100 Hz, where the Methods give 470 and 570 nm at 36 Hz), the mutant ACh sensor is named ACh4.3mut where the paper names ACh3.0-mut, and the session description's reward volume and intervals differ from the Methods. The paper's Figure 8 source data are on Zenodo, not in the dandiset.
